content: The provided text appears to be a list of references from various studies and articles related to contraception, lactation, and associated health outcomes. 1. Contraceptive methods, particularly progestin-only options, have been shown to prevent bone loss in postpartum breastfeeding women. This is critical for maintaining maternal bone health during lactation. 2. The use of a single implant containing elcometrine (ST-1435), a non-orally active progestin, has been evaluated as a long-acting contraceptive for postpartum nursing women, demonstrating efficacy and safety. 3. Comparative studies have assessed the effectiveness of progesterone implants versus placebo and copper intrauterine devices (IUDs) in regulating fertility among breastfeeding women, highlighting the contraceptive benefits of hormonal implants. 4. Observations on the use of depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) in nursing infants and long-term users have provided insights into its effects on lactation and infant health. 5. Research on the influence of Norplant levonorgestrel implants on lactation and infant growth has shown no adverse effects, supporting its use as a contraceptive during breastfeeding. 6. Subdermal progesterone implants have been studied for their contraceptive effectiveness in nursing women, demonstrating reliable prevention of pregnancy without significant impact on lactation. 7. Studies on Norplant implants and progesterone vaginal rings have indicated that these methods do not negatively affect maternal bone turnover or density during lactation and after weaning. 8. The use of progesterone vaginal rings, progestin-only pills, Norplant implants, and copper IUDs has been evaluated for their impact on lactation duration, infant growth, and bleeding patterns, with findings supporting their safety and efficacy. 9. Randomized controlled trials comparing progestin-only contraceptives with combined oral contraceptive pills have examined their effects on lactation, showing that progestin-only methods are compatible with breastfeeding. 10. The administration of norethindrone at a dose of 350 mg has been studied for its effects on lactation and milk composition, with findings indicating no significant adverse outcomes. 11. The impact of various contraceptive methods on lactation has been explored, with evidence suggesting that hormonal and non-hormonal options can be safely used without compromising breastfeeding. 12. Early postpartum use of contraceptive implants has been studied for their effects on lactogenesis, with randomized trials confirming their safety and compatibility with breastfeeding. 13. The administration of progestin-only hormonal contraceptives in the early postpartum period has been compared with non-hormonal methods, showing no significant disruption to short-term breastfeeding patterns. 14. The influence of medroxyprogesterone on breastfeeding duration in urban communities has been studied, with findings supporting its use without adverse effects on lactation. 15. The insertion of levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine contraceptive devices postpartum has been evaluated for its impact on breastfeeding duration and child development, with results indicating no significant negative effects. 16. Long-term follow-up studies of children breastfed by mothers using depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate have shown no adverse developmental outcomes, supporting its safety during lactation. 17. Clinical studies on the effects of steroids on the initiation of lactation have provided evidence that certain hormonal contraceptives can be safely used without impairing milk production. 18. The use of injected progestogens during lactation has been studied, with findings indicating no significant adverse effects on breastfeeding or infant health. 19. The contraceptive efficacy and clinical performance of Nestorone implants in postpartum women have been evaluated, demonstrating their reliability and safety. 20. Studies on the determinants of exclusive breastfeeding in primiparous mothers have highlighted the role of supportive interventions in promoting successful lactation. 21. The effects of progestin-only oral contraceptives on breastfeeding have been compared with non-hormonal methods, showing no significant impact on lactation. 22. Early experiences with new progestogens for contraception have been documented, providing insights into their safety and acceptability among users. 23. Comparative studies of hormonal contraceptives and non-hormonal methods in lactating women have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of progestin-only options. 24. The effects of hormonal contraceptives on milk volume and infant growth have been studied, with findings supporting their compatibility with breastfeeding. 25. The acceptability of progestin-only contraceptives during breastfeeding has been evaluated, showing high levels of user satisfaction and minimal impact on lactation. 26. The effects of hormonal and non-hormonal contraceptives on lactation and pregnancy incidence have been studied, with evidence supporting the safety of hormonal methods during breastfeeding. 27. The use of long-acting contraceptive progestogens has been shown to have no significant adverse effects on lactation, supporting their use in breastfeeding women. 28. Continuous low-dose progestogen administration postpartum has been studied for its ability to maintain lactation while providing effective contraception. 29. The distribution of progesterone receptor immunoreactivity in the fetal and neonatal brain has been studied, providing insights into the potential developmental effects of maternal hormone exposure. 30. The role of progesterone in the developing male brain has been explored, highlighting its importance in neural development and function. 31. The potential gap between bench research and clinical application of progesterone receptors in neural development has been discussed, emphasizing the need for further translational research. 32. The use of levonorgestrel-releasing subdermal capsules (Norplant) after pregnancy termination has been evaluated, showing effective contraception and a return to fertility after removal. 33. Immediate post-abortal contraception with Norplant has been studied, with findings indicating effective prevention of pregnancy and a return to normal hormonal levels after removal. 34. Post-abortal contraception with norethisterone enanthate injections has been evaluated, demonstrating effective prevention of pregnancy and compatibility with lactation. 35. The use of levonorgestrel intrauterine devices and Norplant for immediate post-abortal contraception has been studied, showing high efficacy and safety. 36. Prospective studies on weight changes in new users of hormonal contraceptives have provided insights into the potential metabolic effects of these methods. 37. The effects of progestin-only long-acting contraceptives on metabolic markers in obese women have been studied, showing no significant adverse outcomes. 38. Changes in weight and body composition associated with injectable and oral contraceptive use have been documented, providing evidence for their safety in terms of metabolic health. 39. The relationship between early weight gain and later weight changes in users of depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate has been studied, highlighting the importance of monitoring weight in adolescent users. 40. The effects of hormonal contraceptives on weight, fat mass, and fat distribution have been studied, showing no significant long-term adverse effects. 41. The safety and efficacy of DMPA-SC as a contraceptive agent have been evaluated, demonstrating its reliability and acceptability among users. 42. Preliminary findings on the side effects of Norplant in adolescents have been documented, providing insights into its safety and tolerability. 43. The effects of hormonal contraceptives on cardiovascular health have been studied, with findings supporting their safety in most users. 44. The risk of venous thromboembolism in users of progestin-only contraceptives has been evaluated, showing a low incidence rate. 45. The use of levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems in managing menorrhagia in women with hemostatic disorders has been studied, demonstrating significant benefits. 46. The incidence rates of arterial and venous thrombosis in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus have been documented, providing insights into the safety of contraceptive use in this population. 47. Trials of contraceptive methods in women with systemic lupus erythematosus have been conducted, showing the safety and efficacy of various options. 48. Combined oral contraceptives in women with systemic lupus erythematosus have been studied, demonstrating their safety and effectiveness in preventing pregnancy.
